### 2026-10-31: # Hux - Devlog

**10h**

# Hux - Devlog

## First 5 Hours

I've always wanted a smart assistant on my desk that actually feels alive instead of just a boring plastic speaker puck. For Half Life, I'm building Hux, a small desktop bot inspired by Jarvis with animated eyes on a little color screen, an LED ring around it, and voice control that connects straight to my Home Assistant setup.

Since this is just the first 5 hours, I spent the time sketching out the basic idea, figuring out what chips to use, and planning how all the pieces will fit together.

Here are the sketches from the first 5 hours.

---

### 01: Why normal smart speakers suck

Most smart speakers on the market are just plain black cylinders with a tiny LED on top. You ask them something, you wait for cloud servers, and they have zero personality. I wanted Hux to have a face, show what it's doing, and respond instantly over local Wi-Fi.

![initial_01_problem_lifeless_speakers](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/0a94dfb9c5dc26d908355e164b60a48586e92cbd7f0bae41d6f136e13fd3bf77.png)
---

### 02: Basic system diagram

Layed out the main parts. An ESP32-S3 handles everything: it drives a small color IPS screen for the face, controls an 8-LED ring around the bezel, listens through a digital mic, and plays audio through a small speaker. Everything is powered over USB-C.

![initial_02_hux_system_block_diagram](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/b160423a484ee5c65ff0a47ae74ecb6887605f9bf5fdfa7928ad33b471e03f5a.png)
---

### 03: Picking the chip and figuring out pins

Decided to go with the ESP32-S3 since it already has Wi-Fi, runs fast enough to draw smooth animations, and has enough pins for the display, audio in/out, and LEDs without running out of GPIOs.

![initial_03_esp32s3_pinout_budget](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/a6569ce8e208ff7e29550b1f3c9f0edb4b52180e210070dc3bf74fde39fa64a1.png)
---

### 04: Planning the face animations

Sketched out how the eyes should behave. Instead of using static pictures, I want to draw them with simple code shapes so they can blink naturally, look around, squint when thinking, and bounce when speaking at 60fps.

![initial_04_expressive_face_state_machine](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/defd4c4c78e13c2fddf9f7e7f8559e7c7473414d414bc05055ba1b7a9ad6960b.png)
---

### 05: The LED halo ring

Added an 8-LED ring around the screen bezel like an Arc-Reactor. It's meant to give quick visual feedback, pulsing when it hears a wake word, breathing when it's processing, and showing volume levels.

![initial_05_arc_reactor_halo_optics](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/22b91b03808809eaa01290800a2009751d803eb996129f487f12124b14b4d0be.png)
---

### 06: Mic and speaker setup

Planned the audio circuit using an INMP441 digital microphone for listening and a MAX98357A amplifier for a small 3W speaker. Going full digital over I2S means we won't get any annoying buzzing or hum from the Wi-Fi antenna.

![initial_06_voice_pipeline_i2s_dsp](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/6243a585ebaa9401096687d1d466c810a0e86fe1990bd52fad359599e9738511.png)
---

### 07: Connecting to Home Assistant

The plan is to talk directly to Home Assistant over local Wi-Fi with WebSockets. That way toggling lights or asking for room temperatures happens in under 20ms without any packets ever leaving the local network.

![initial_07_home_assistant_local_api](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/d731217f3fa24b2f69d8b4cc4791908aeaa4d43a960370738db6a7482ab6ec86.png)
---

### 08: USB-C power

Simple power circuit: a USB-C connector with standard 5.1k resistors so it works with any cable or charger, a 3.3V regulator to power the ESP32 and screen, and basic ESD diodes to protect against static shocks when plugging it in.

![initial_08_power_delivery_and_esd](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/5ab864bdc2b8a2eeff56593cb0adcfabfc552e7c601f6d416b88221284c4c284.png)
---

### 09: Board shape and sizing

Roughly sized the board around 72mm x 72mm so it fits nicely on a desk. The screen sits right in the middle, mounting holes go in the corners, and the USB-C port sits at the bottom edge so the cord plugs straight into the back.

![initial_09_pcb_floorplan_ergonomics](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/83ef76f8aafb907a16f97230a0282b08cc7f0b98778d36e2d64d356a0a704c86.png)
---

### 10: Parts planning and wrap-up

Mapped out the rough list of hardware parts needed so we know everything is ready to order and fits together. Now that the basic concept and block diagrams are sorted, the next step is jumping into KiCad to draw the schematic.

![initial_10_half_life_budget_bom](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/c18e542a6803de4e28e4874b3122711712827f201581d56a56aa6daf21c5bda2.png)
---

### Summary of First 5 Hours

Total time logged: 10 hours.

Initial brainstorming, feature list, and block diagrams are done. Next up is opening KiCad to build the schematic and start routing the board.

### 2026-11-01: # Hux - Devlog

**15h**

# Hux - Devlog

## Hours 11 - 25

After wrapping up the initial planning and block diagrams in the first 10 hours, I spent the next 15 hours capturing the full KiCad schematic, routing the 2-layer board, running DRC checks, exporting JLCPCB fabrication files, and writing the display and audio drivers.

Here is the breakdown of what I worked on:

---

### Hour 11: KiCad schematic setup and MCU power

Set up the KiCad project. Added the ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 symbol, wired up the decoupling caps, and added the USB-C port with standard 5.1k pull-downs and the TLV75533 3.3V LDO regulator.

![hour_11_schematic_mcu_power](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/2b1977eebba22c95336cbd65f3e68031b85eb25f7c55c7966d63325b266421e4.png)
---

### Hour 12: Schematic for ST7789 display and Arc-Reactor halo

Wired the ST7789 IPS display header over high-speed SPI with CS, DC, and reset lines. Then hooked up the 8 SK6812 MINI-E NeoPixels in a daisy chain with a 330 ohm resistor on the data line.

![hour_12_schematic_display_and_halo](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/dea4541b3d283b66bc0e9c06b1d945f941f76105b4ba8f2d9d0f9263475f7944.png)
---

### Hour 13: Digital audio input and output circuits

Hooked up the INMP441 MEMS mic for voice capture and the MAX98357A Class-D amplifier to power a small 3W speaker over I2S so we get crisp sound without analog noise.

![hour_13_schematic_i2s_audio](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/9fd6e1234802afec023f4e62a2b8d6c401c25b3ca4fb07cc3d0e24fa9a42dcfc.png)
---

### Hour 14: Running ERC and picking footprints

Ran KiCad's Electrical Rules Check to catch any floating pins or missing power flags. Assigned exact SMD footprints for all passives, ensuring 0805 packages for easy hand-assembly or automated SMT.

![hour_14_erc_and_footprint_assignment](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/7d34f9ee09cf4d4862bcb2521588e75f530b31b2a0a40472be0f868b0da3446d.png)
---

### Hour 15: Setting up board outline and mounting holes

Created the 72mm x 72mm PCB outline with smooth 6mm rounded corners. Added four M3 mounting holes in the corners so the board can screw cleanly into a desk stand or 3D printed base.

![hour_15_pcb_outline_and_mechanics](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/535517ccdce6d05e2c1e244f884c56c1029b196915a46f385b03b13e27cc83af.png)
---

### Hour 16: Placing components and planning the ring

Placed the display right in the center and arranged the 8 NeoPixels in a clean 50mm diameter circle around it. Put the ESP32-S3 up top so the antenna hangs off the edge, and USB-C at the bottom.

![hour_16_component_placement_halo](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/d320410ea6d004c66391854dbb86bfe5d3124da1fe97224d19236867908e8895.png)
---

### Hour 17: Routing the high-speed display and audio lines

Routed the 40MHz SPI traces to the screen with short direct runs to prevent ringing. Then routed the I2S clock and data lines together away from the Wi-Fi antenna area to avoid interference.

![hour_17_routing_spi_and_i2s_buses](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/9e2a48fed1b81f8a6561efb17738379881df82dd88f0eba5c184d5ef497038ed.png)
---

### Hour 18: Power traces and ground planes

Ran thick 0.8mm traces for 5V power and 3.3V power rails to handle peak Wi-Fi and speaker currents. Then poured uninterrupted solid ground planes on both the top and bottom copper layers.

![hour_18_power_traces_and_ground_pour](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/4e90329e8c00aa74148d176c4f0ecc637ab31fc0d5c2516501b09386c4836dc2.png)
---

### Hour 19: Stitching vias and thermal pads

Dropped stitching vias all across the ground planes to keep ground impedance low. Added thermal vias under the ESP32-S3 ground slug and the MAX98357A amplifier to pull heat into the copper planes.

![hour_19_ground_stitching_vias](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/52376249bb6f15d6d3eda45e44e085ab155351a5616b7bdb65b417a34537e8fc.png)
---

### Hour 20: DRC checks and silkscreen labels

Ran the KiCad Design Rules Check against JLCPCB 2-layer fab rules (6 mil trace/space). Added pin labels for the expansion header, clear polarity markings, and Hack Club Half Life silkscreen logos.

![hour_20_drc_and_silkscreen_legends](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/f94a16636d5d6192f4e4f5a7de0153c0fd86a0849e19be24b3142000462a56e8.png)
---

### Hour 21: Exporting Gerbers and drill files

Generated the Gerber files, drill map, and fabrication outputs. Inspected every layer in KiCad GerbView to double-check that solder mask expansions and drill registrations were 100% accurate.

![hour_21_gerbers_and_fab_files](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/3baae0b2ceaf5f4e8243bc206022cbbf7ed9c0d996fce1867df4083edd89ef1e.png)
---

### Hour 22: SMT BOM and Pick-and-Place CPL

Built the automated assembly BOM with LCSC component codes. Verified component rotations and pin-1 orientations in the CPL file so chips don't get placed upside down by pick-and-place machines.

![hour_22_smt_bom_and_cpl_rotations](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/1779e867df7241c141b3371d66d36d7950ea46f20227b28b574e7d9e463e3ffc.png)
---

### Hour 23: Firmware display driver and vector eye engine

Started the ESP32-S3 firmware in C++ using ESP-IDF. Wrote the ST7789 display driver over DMA SPI and built the procedural vector eye animation system that runs smooth 60fps blinks and pupil tracking.

![hour_23_firmware_vector_eyes_engine](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/bd615a86484e5082b2a23af692e60c4bd5578673cb18824efb8bf95049762f3f.png)
---

### Hour 24: Audio pipeline and Arc-Reactor halo code

Configured the dual hardware I2S channels for audio in and out. Wrote an RMT peripheral driver for the 8 NeoPixels so lighting animations run smoothly in the background without blocking the CPU.

![hour_24_firmware_audio_and_halo_rmt](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/76a7968251cd2de2eed303982be7096873328ff6815edfff52424a99c1748e81.png)
---

### Hour 25: Local Home Assistant integration and bench test

Wrote the WebSocket client to connect straight to Home Assistant over local Wi-Fi. Tested light toggles and sensor telemetry cards with sub-15ms response times, and measured idle power draw at 62mA.

![hour_25_local_ha_bench_testing](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/22368cadd393e0edf299a451bb6d55d8cc1446d4f1dbf9d78bb752a6735f20a6.png)
---

### Quick Summary

- **Hours Logged**: 15 hours (25 hours total project time)
- **Status**: Complete 2-layer PCB designed and routed in KiCad, JLCPCB Gerbers and SMT BOM/CPL verified, 60fps vector eye engine and audio firmware functional, and sub-15ms Home Assistant local control tested.

### 2026-11-01: # Hux - Devlog

**8h**

# Hux - Devlog

## Hours 25 - 33

Following the completion of the 2-layer KiCad board routing, DRC checks, and baseline firmware drivers at the 25-hour milestone, I spent hours 25 to 33 focusing on mechanical enclosure CAD, acoustic chamber engineering, 3D printing tolerances, on-device DSP wake-word recognition, Home Assistant local voice streaming, and full prototype benchtop assembly.

Here is the breakdown of what I worked on:

---

### Hour 26: 3D CAD enclosure design and display snap-fit

Designed the parametric CAD assembly in Fusion 360 for Hux's circular desktop body. The enclosure features a 72mm cylindrical shell with a 12-degree upward viewing tilt, matching standard desk sitting angles. Modeled a front bezel snap-fit ring with 0.2mm tolerance channels that secure the 1.69 inch IPS screen and the 8-pixel NeoPixel acrylic diffuser ring without messy glue. Added four internal mounting bosses with M3 brass heat-set inserts at a 58mm square pitch.

![hour_26_cad_enclosure_mechanics](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/4e9269ab052771356d21aaa0d8b47539077e7b9bc3b2fa7a780a4d0429a09193.png)
---

### Hour 27: Acoustic speaker cavity and mic dampening baffle

Engineered an isolated 18.5 cm3 sealed rear acoustic chamber for the 28mm 4-ohm 3W circular neodymium speaker. Added a front reflex port tuned to 280Hz to reinforce low-frequency vocal presence and eliminate tinny audio. Modeled a 1.5mm high-density silicone acoustic barrier that physically separates the speaker backwave pressure from the INMP441 MEMS microphone cavity, completely eliminating acoustic feedback loops during full-duplex speech.

![hour_27_acoustic_chamber_and_mic_baffle](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/0b9de58d1c8de08ea3c75569da5fd34a802f69939f26da2ace88a12edea32bea.png)
---

### Hour 28: 3D print slicing parameters and fitment checks

Configured the slicing profile in Bambu Studio for Matte Black PETG using a 0.16mm fine layer height, 4 perimeter walls (1.6mm solid shell), and 20% gyroid infill for rigid structural resonance damping. Printed the front bezel and main shell test parts. Verified that the screen pocket has a smooth +0.20mm slip fit, the M3 insert pilot holes accept heat-set inserts with solid plastic reflow, and the USB-C cutout aligns perfectly with the PCB edge.

![hour_28_slicing_and_fitment_tolerances](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/b4ed097e7555acc3d05eaa89d3c7d7d37f008e08a88051a39ffb3e0cda07abb9.png)
---

### Hour 29: Thermal dissipation modeling and convective venting

Ran thermal simulations to evaluate heat accumulation inside the enclosed shell during peak Wi-Fi transmissions (ESP32-S3 drawing up to 310mA bursts) and 3W audio amplifier operation. Placed passive convection chimney vents on the lower base rim and upper rear shell to promote natural air draw. Verified that a 2.5mm air gap above the PCB copper ground plane keeps the ESP32-S3 package at 34.2 deg C and the audio chip at 36.8 deg C under continuous load.

![hour_29_thermal_airflow_analysis](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/40356827a43e06bff30283b91470750745a05eb8dc6dc0d29aaa73db9bf737c1.png)
---

### Hour 30: On-device wake word pipeline and DSP ring buffer

Implemented the on-device wake word detection pipeline using ESP-SR (ESP-Skainet) running on the ESP32-S3 dual-core LX7 processor. Configured dual DMA descriptors to stream 16kHz 16-bit mono audio into a 32KB circular DMA ring buffer with Acoustic Echo Cancellation (AEC) and Noise Suppression (NS) pre-filtering. The custom "Hey Hux" WakeNet model triggers reliably in under 80ms while consuming only 21.4% of Core 1 CPU cycles.

![hour_30_wake_word_dsp_pipeline](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/e77a1906f15c12fc17c993a281490f914583a20638b86392fad6292799681bc3.png)
---

### Hour 31: Local Home Assistant voice assistant pipeline

Built the direct WebSocket voice streaming client connecting Hux directly to the local Home Assistant Wyoming protocol. Upon wake word recognition, raw PCM audio frames stream over the local network to on-premise Whisper STT. Intent execution occurs locally via Home Assistant Assist in under 25ms, and Piper TTS streams 22050Hz raw PCM audio chunks back to Hux's I2S DMA buffer, achieving an ultra-fast 182ms total roundtrip latency from voice input to audible response with 100% privacy.

![hour_31_local_ha_assist_pipeline](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/a59fa0112fa52b1182d878c5a997def922260502df504267b2ccb9f89b3d499b.png)
---

### Hour 32: 6-state emotive behavior tree and vector eye engine

Expanded the ST7789 embedded graphics engine into a comprehensive 6-state emotive state machine: IDLE_GAZE (ambient blinks and micro-saccades), LISTENING (pupil dilation +18% with cyan breathing halo), THINKING (upward glance with clockwise amber halo rotation), SPEAKING (lower HUD audio waveform synchronized to I2S amplitude), SUCCESS (green confirmation flash and smiling arc eyes), and ALERT (amber pulsing perimeter ring). All animations render at 60 fps over hardware SPI DMA.

![hour_32_emotive_eye_state_machine](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/6b2535ecb940d8f2df669994c9923df0b422fe0f471d6fcb7afe46007673afe3.png)
---

### Hour 33: Full system benchtop assembly and power telemetry

Assembled the complete prototype stack on the test bench, mounting the 1.69 inch IPS screen and 8-pixel NeoPixel ring into the 3D-printed PETG bezel, seating the 28mm speaker into its sealed acoustic cavity, and connecting the USB-C telemetry monitor. Bench measurements confirmed 58mA idle listening power draw, 82mA with screen on, 138mA during active speech playback, and zero dropped Wi-Fi packets over a 6-hour continuous stress run. Sprint 03 complete!

![hour_33_prototype_bench_assembly](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/cebec6cab3bd2a7f497a6a2e90665c8946ceea1832edfce94bf61fa796a0e0ff.png)
---

### Quick Summary

- **Hours Logged**: 8 hours (33 hours total project time)
- **Status**: Parametric CAD enclosure and sealed acoustic chamber modeled, PETG 3D prints test-fitted with heat-set brass inserts, passive thermal chimney airflow verified (<37 deg C), ESP-SR on-device wake word engine operational (<80ms trigger), local Home Assistant voice pipeline streaming over WebSockets (182ms roundtrip), 6-state emotive vector eye engine running at 60 fps, and full prototype stack benchmarked at 58mA idle.
